headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared filesystem/MCP and broad tool access; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, and agent_b can read/write the VS Code workspace plus use MCP. That creates a direct content bridge where agent_a outputs can be consumed by agent_b as instructions, and agent_b’s browser/file content can be fed back. Shared channels and permissive tool parsing make injection plausible by default.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions into files or MCP messages that agent_b reads, injection is possible.
IF agent_b ingests workspace text or browser content as trusted prompts, attacker-controlled content can steer actions.
mitigations: Disable automatic prompt ingestion from files and MCP outputs.
Separate workspaces so agent_a and agent_b do not share writable paths.
Require explicit human review before agent_b acts on agent_a-produced text.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization at the MCP boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures, while agent_b reads and writes workspace files and has broad network egress. Because agent_b shares state via filesystem and can call external model APIs, sensitive content from agent_a can leak through the shared workspace or outbound requests. The pairwise pathway is documented by the profiles, so uncertainty is limited.
conditions: IF agent_a stores prompts, signatures, or repository metadata in the shared workspace, agent_b can read them.
IF agent_b forwards workspace contents to its configured model API, those contents can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Move secrets and prompts out of the shared workspace.
Restrict agent_b network egress to approved endpoints only.
Use separate OS users or containers for each agent.
Redact secrets before either agent writes to disk.
requires-engineering: add per-file access controls and outbound content filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, install packages, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. agent_b explicitly shares state with other instances via filesystem, while agent_a can also modify git state. Concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace can corrupt files, race git operations, or overwrite each other without locking, which is dangerous in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or workspace, write conflicts can occur.
IF either agent performs git operations without external locking, repository state can be corrupted.
mitigations: Run the agents in separate clones or workspaces.
Serialize git and filesystem writes with a lock file.
Assign only one agent write authority per directory.
Pause one agent during package installs or branch changes.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a’s sandboxing describes background analysis tasks and route/explain/build-agents commands, while agent_b has browser access and can act on workspace files. If agent_b treats agent_a’s outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade into code changes, browser actions, or commits. The pairwise interaction is plausible by default and the blast radius includes downstream actions, so higher severity is warranted.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without verification, incorrect facts can propagate into actions.
IF agent_a emits malformed or speculative analysis, agent_b may commit or execute it.
mitigations: Require a verification step before agent_b acts on agent_a output.
Limit agent_a to advisory-only outputs.
Log and diff all agent_a-to-agent_b handoffs.
Block direct commit or browser actions from unreviewed agent_a outputs.
requires-engineering: add structured schemas and validation gates.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles task prompts, repository metadata, and signatures; agent_b handles source code and browser screenshots. Both are open-source and docs-only, but agent_b’s broad network egress and model-API calls can move workspace data outside the local environment, creating retention and residency ambiguity. No specific residency certification mismatch is documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace, outbound API calls may create a compliance issue.
IF retention policies differ between local files and external model providers, deletion/export obligations may be inconsistent.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents’ workspaces.
Disable external model calls for regulated projects.
Document retention and deletion handling for each provider.
Use region-locked endpoints where available.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing and retention controls.
